title-group.article-title: Bladder-sparing chemoradiotherapy following neoadjuvant chemotherapy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a retrospective cohort study

sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Radical cystectomy following cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is still the standard approach for managing muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC); however, a substantial proportion of patients are not candidates for surgery or cisplatin-based chemotherapy. The role of NAC followed by chemoradiation (CRT) in a bladder-preserving approach is not well established. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, survival outcomes, and prognostic factors associated with NAC followed by definitive CRT.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: We retrospectively analyzed MIBC patients treated with NAC and subsequent CRT between 2010 and 2023. Overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) were analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 224 MIBC patients treated with NAC, 132 patients received bladder-preserving CRT after NAC. The median OS for the entire cohort was 58 months (95% CI: 37.63–78.37). Median OS was significantly longer in patients with clinical complete response (cCR) compared with those without (73 vs. 29 months, p = 0.007). Median EFS was also superior in the cCR group (50 vs. 23 months, p = 0.022). In multivariable Cox regression analysis, achievement of cCR was independently associated with superior OS (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.30–0.92, p = 0.028) and EFS (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32–0.93, p = 0.036). Moreover, the presence of baseline hydronephrosis predicted significantly worse OS (HR 2.37, 95% CI 1.32–4.25, p = 0.006) but showed no association with EFS. The type of NAC regimen (cisplatin vs. carboplatin) had no independent effect on survival.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: NAC followed by CRT is a feasible bladder-preserving approach for selected patients with MIBC, including those ineligible for cystectomy or cisplatin. Achievement of cCR is the most robust prognostic factor for both OS and EFS, supporting its role as a surrogate endpoint in this setting. These findings provide novel evidence for integrating NAC into bladder-preserving strategies and highlight clinical factors that may guide individualized treatment selection. A prospective randomized trial is warranted.
Keywords: Bladder malignancy, Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, Chemoradiotherapy, Overall survival

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) remains a highly aggressive disease with a substantial risk of recurrence and mortality despite multimodal management [1, 2]. Radical cystectomy with perioperative cisplatin-based chemotherapy has long been considered the standard of care for eligible patients [3, 4]. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) before surgery has demonstrated a clear overall survival (OS) benefit and is recommended in international guidelines [3]. However, many patients are either medically unfit for cystectomy or decline surgery due to its morbidity and impact on quality of life [5, 6].

Bladder-preserving approaches using chemoradiotherapy (CRT) emerged as an effective alternative for selected patients, providing comparable oncologic outcomes with the potential for organ preservation [7, 8]. Existing evidence from small institutional series and retrospective studies indicates that NAC before CRT may yield promising outcomes; however, validation is still lacking [9–11]. The integration of NAC with CRT provides both systemic and local therapeutic advantages. Early administration of chemotherapy facilitates the eradication of micrometastatic disease, thereby reducing the risk of distant relapse. Subsequent radiotherapy, applied after tumor cytoreduction by chemotherapy, enhances local control by more effectively targeting residual tumor cells. Moreover, this combined strategy may enable organ preservation, minimizing the need for radical surgical interventions while maintaining oncologic efficacy. However, the role of NAC prior to CRT in MIBC patients is less clearly defined in the literature.

Moreover, approximately 30–50% of patients with MIBC are ineligible for cisplatin-based chemotherapy, necessitating alternative systemic regimens such as gemcitabine plus carboplatin, for which data in the bladder-preservation context are scarce [12].

Given this gap in evidence, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with MIBC who received NAC followed by definitive chemoradiation. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the feasibility and survival outcomes of NAC, particularly in cisplatin-ineligible, surgery-unfit, or cystectomy-declining patients. We also explored clinical factors that may inform patient selection for bladder-preserving strategies. Our findings provide new evidence supporting the integration of NAC with chemoradiation and highlight opportunities to refine risk stratification and optimize individualized treatment planning for patients pursuing bladder preservation.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: In this retrospective cohort study, data were collected from all consecutive patients with MIBC (T2–T4aN0–1M0) who received CRT after the platinum-based NAC in two tertiary hospitals in Tehran, Iran, between February 2010 and February 2023. The diagnosis of urothelial cell carcinoma was established based on transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) findings. All included tumors were diagnosed as urothelial carcinoma based on TURBT pathology. A very small subset of patients exhibited minor variant histological features (e.g., squamous differentiation), but no patients with predominant non-urothelial histologies (such as small-cell, adenocarcinoma, or sarcomatoid carcinoma) were included. Initial staging was performed using contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. MRI was used when CT was contraindicated. Nodal status was confirmed histologically when feasible. FDG PET/CT was used infrequently. Patient selection for NAC was based on tumor stage (≥ T2), performance status, renal function, and multidisciplinary team decision-making. Demographic characteristics, clinical and pathological features, treatment regimens, and outcomes were obtained from medical records. Specifically, patients with extensive CIS, bilateral hydronephrosis persisting after NAC, small bladder capacity, prior pelvic radiotherapy, Crohn’s disease, or active inflammatory bowel disease were excluded from CRT. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (IR.SBMU.UNRC.REC. 1403.002). Due to the retrospective design, the Ethics Committee waived the requirement for informed consent.

sec.title: Treatment protocol
sec.p: For NAC, patients with performance status 0–1 and creatinine clearance > 60 mL/min (calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault equation) received cisplatin at 35 mg/m² over 60 min on days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle, combined with gemcitabine 1250 mg/m² intravenously over 30 min on days 1 and 8, for up to four cycles. Patients with performance status 2, creatinine clearance ≤ 60 mL/min, or hydronephrosis were instead treated with carboplatin (AUC = 4, intravenously over 30 min) on day 1 every 21 days, together with gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² intravenously over 30 min on days 1 and 8, also for up to four cycles. Carboplatin doses were adjusted according to renal function using the Cockcroft-Gault formula.

Four weeks after completion of NAC, all patients were scheduled for cystoscopic assessment, with repeat TURBT or targeted tumor-site biopsy performed as indicated. Clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as the absence of a detectable primary tumor (T0), as confirmed by cystoscopy, negative urine cytology, and no evidence of residual disease on cross-sectional imaging [13]. Patients who were considered ineligible for surgery (e.g., patients with cardiovascular disease) or those who declined radical cystectomy underwent CRT, particularly if they achieved a cCR after NAC. Radiotherapy was tailored according to nodal status: node-negative patients received whole-bladder irradiation to a total dose of 64 Gy, whereas node-positive patients received 45 Gy to the bladder and pelvic lymph nodes, followed by a bladder boost to reach a total dose of 64 Gy. Radiotherapy was delivered five days per week at 1.8 Gy per fraction. Concurrent chemotherapy consisted of mitomycin 12 mg/m² on day 1, plus fluorouracil 1000 mg/m² on days 1–3, and 16–18 of radiotherapy. Surveillance after CRT included regular cystoscopic evaluation in accordance with oncological guidelines, urine cytology, and cross-sectional imaging (e.g., CT/MRI). Recurrences were managed according to disease extent and patient fitness, including salvage cystectomy or chemotherapy.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: In accordance with recommendations for MIBC patients receiving NAC, overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) were chosen as the study endpoints [13, 14]. OS was defined as the interval from the initiation of NAC to death from any cause, with patients without an event censored at their last follow-up. EFS was defined as the time from the first day of NAC to the earliest occurrence of disease progression during or after NAC, local or distant recurrence following definitive local therapy, or death from any cause. Patients who did not experience any of these events were censored at their last follow-up.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Survival outcomes, including OS and EFS, were summarized as median survival times in months and estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with differences between groups assessed by the log-rank test. Follow-up duration was assessed using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. To identify predictors of OS and EFS, univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were applied. Following the rule of thumb relative to the number of events, the five variables showing the strongest associations in univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable models. Bootstrapping with 1000 resamples was used for internal validation. Gender and tumor grade were not suitable for inclusion in the models due to the predominance of male patients and high-grade tumors. No strong correlations (r ≥ 0.7) were observed among the independent variables. Also, chi-square analysis did not demonstrate any statistically significant associations between baseline clinicopathologic variables and the achievement of cCR. Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 23 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), with a two-sided p-value < 0.05 defined as the threshold for statistical significance.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: A total of 224 patients with MIBC who underwent NAC before CRT or RC were assessed. Of these, 132 patients treated with CRT and followed for at least 24 months were included in the available-case analysis. The median follow-up time was 54 months (95%CI: 48.53–59.47).

Baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1. More than half of the patients (57.6%) were older than 65 years, and the cohort was predominantly male (89.4%). Most patients received the gemcitabine/carboplatin (Gem/Carbo) regimen (56.1%). A cCR following neoadjuvant chemotherapy was achieved in 64.4% of patients. Hydronephrosis was present in 20.5%, and impaired renal function (creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min) was documented in 60.6%.

sec.title: Overall survival
sec.p: The entire cohort had a median OS of 58 months (95% CI: 37.63–78.37). In univariable analysis (Table 2), absence of cCR, presence of hydronephrosis, older age (> 65 years), and reduced creatinine clearance (< 60 mL/min) were significantly associated with inferior OS. Kaplan–Meier survival curves for the significant predictors of OS, as well as for the entire cohort, are presented in Fig. 1. Median OS was 73 months (95% CI 35.5–110.5) for patients achieving cCR compared with 29 months (95% CI 10.8–47.2) in those without cCR (p = 0.007). Similarly, median OS was significantly longer in patients without hydronephrosis (88 months, 95% CI 49.2–126.8) than in those with hydronephrosis (41 months, 95% CI 19.9–62.1; p = 0.005). Median OS also favored younger patients (≤ 65 years: 88 months vs. >65 years: 41 months; p = 0.007) and those with preserved renal function (≥ 60 mL/min: 76 months vs. <60 mL/min: 43 months; p = 0.024). On multivariable analysis, cCR (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.30–0.92; p = 0.028) and hydronephrosis (HR 2.37, 95% CI 1.32–4.25; p = 0.006) remained independently associated with OS.

sec.title: Event-free survival
sec.p: Across the entire cohort, the median EFS was 42 months (95% CI: 22.89–61.11). In univariable analysis for EFS (Table 3), absence of cCR and older age were associated with worse outcomes. Kaplan–Meier survival curves illustrating the significant predictors of EFS, along with the curve for the entire cohort, are shown in Fig. 2. Median EFS was 50 months (95% CI 28.5–71.4) in patients achieving cCR versus 23 months (95% CI 15.0–30.9) in those without cCR (p = 0.022). Age also significantly impacted EFS, with a median EFS of 60 months (95% CI 43.2–76.8) in patients ≤ 65 years versus 26 months (95% CI 15.4–36.6) in those > 65 years (p = 0.022). In multivariable analysis, cCR remained a significant predictor (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32–0.93; p = 0.036).

sec.title: Rationale and potential advantages
sec.p: To date, the role of NAC in the bladder-preserving setting remains a topic of debate. While NAC has been shown to improve survival in patients undergoing cystectomy [4], its additional value when followed by CRT is less well defined (9–11). The rationale for this approach lies in its potential to optimize both systemic and local disease control. By delivering chemotherapy upfront, occult micrometastatic disease can be addressed at an earlier stage, thereby reducing the likelihood of distant relapse. In addition, cytoreduction achieved through NAC may enhance the efficacy of subsequent radiotherapy, which can then be administered to a smaller tumor burden, potentially improving locoregional control and limiting radiation toxicity. Beyond these oncologic benefits, the sequential combination of NAC and CRT offers the additional advantage of facilitating organ preservation in selected patients, reducing the need for radical surgical interventions without compromising treatment outcomes. Such an approach is particularly relevant in malignancies where functional outcomes and quality of life are closely tied to organ conservation. Nevertheless, the heterogeneity of existing data and the absence of large randomized trials highlight the need for further investigations to establish the true clinical value of this combined modality strategy.

sec.title: Comparison with prior studies
sec.p: Single-institution reports and retrospective series have shown that delivering cisplatin-based NAC before selective bladder-sparing CRT is feasible with survival times comparable to those observed in our cohort [9–11]. Jiang et al. [9] reported that NAC followed by CRT was associated with encouraging bladder-preservation rates and survival outcomes in 57 nonmetastatic MIBC, supporting the feasibility of this approach; however, the median follow-up time was 19.3 months. Also, Sung et al. [10] evaluated 64 patients with MIBC over a median follow-up of 34 months, and reported that administering a Gem/Cis NAC regimen before bladder-preservation CRT resulted in favorable oncologic outcomes, supporting its potential use in clinical practice. Halabi et al. [11] further contributed to this evidence by comparing cystectomy with bladder preservation after NAC and showing that, in selected patients, bladder-sparing strategies did not compromise survival outcomes. In their study, no significant difference was noted in the OS and disease-free survival (DFS) between the groups who underwent RC post-NAC (26 patients) and CRT post-NAC (18 patients). The mean follow-up times were 25 and 22.7 months for the RC post-NAC and CRT post-NAC groups, respectively. Compared with these prior institutional experiences, our cohort size is relatively larger and provides additional supportive evidence for the role of NAC as a selection tool for bladder preservation strategies. Moreover, these earlier series were limited by short follow-up durations, whereas our analysis offers more mature data. Importantly, our study extends this evidence by demonstrating that achieving cCR after NAC is a strong predictor of both OS and EFS in patients subsequently treated with CRT. Taken together, the existing literature and our findings suggest a consistent pattern: NAC may be effectively integrated into bladder-preservation approaches to identify clinical responders and reduce the risk of systemic relapse. However, the true magnitude of benefit and the optimal criteria for patient selection remain to be established in prospective randomized trials.

sec.title: The prognostic significance of cCR
sec.p: Our adjusted analyses demonstrate that achieving a cCR after NAC is a robust prognostic factor, independently associated with improved OS and EFS. The prognostic significance of cCR is consistent with prior studies using NAC in MIBC patients [15–17]. Wu et al. [18] further emphasize that cCR following NAC not only correlates with favorable survival outcomes but also represents a critical determinant in guiding subsequent disease management strategies. They concluded that bladder preservation in patients achieving cCR after NAC is gaining recognition as a novel treatment approach. Our results extend these observations by highlighting cCR as a robust surrogate endpoint in patients treated with NAC followed by CRT, supporting its use as a biomarker for risk stratification and treatment adaptation. It should be noted that the term cCR is most commonly used to describe tumor eradication following definitive curative-intent treatment, such as CRT in bladder-preservation protocols. In the present study, cCR was used to describe the absence of detectable residual primary tumor following NAC. We acknowledge that this represents an interim response assessment rather than a definitive post-curative outcome. Nevertheless, achieving a cCR after NAC has been consistently shown to correlate with favorable oncological outcomes and is clinically relevant, as it influences subsequent treatment decisions, including eligibility for bladder-preserving approaches versus early radical cystectomy. Lee et al. [19] provided a comprehensive discussion of both the clinical possibilities and the inherent limitations of assessing cCR following NAC in patients with MIBC.

sec.title: Hydronephrosis and patient selection
sec.p: Hydronephrosis emerged as a strong negative prognostic factor, independently associated with shorter OS, highlighting the importance of careful patient selection in bladder-preserving protocols [20–22]. Previous studies have shown that patients with hydronephrosis have lower rates of complete response and survival, and thus are generally not candidates for bladder preservation [21]. Also, in patients treated with trimodal therapy (TMT), hydronephrosis was an important predictor of OS [20, 22]. Our observation aligns with prior literature indicating that hydronephrosis predicts reduced survival time. Importantly, a recent study specifically evaluated the impact of CRT on pre-existing hydronephrosis in patients undergoing bladder-preserving treatment [23].

sec.title: Cisplatin eligibility and the role of carboplatin
sec.p: Up to 50% of bladder cancer patients are ineligible for cisplatin [24, 25]. For these patients, carboplatin-based regimens have been considered, though evidence in MIBC is limited [15, 26–30]. Retrospective data suggest a potential benefit of carboplatin-based NAC compared with cystectomy alone [27–29]. Murasawa et al. [27] showed improvements in OS and DFS with Gem/Carbo compared to RC alone in cisplatin-ineligible patients. Besides, Koie et al. [28] indicated that neoadjuvant Gem/Carbo chemotherapy followed by immediate cystectomy could enhance OS and DFS in patients with cT2 MIBC, compared with radical cystectomy alone. They also reported reduced recurrence rates for the Gem/Carbo regimen [29]. More recently, larger multicenter and institutional series have compared Gem/Carbo with the standard Gem/Cis regimen in the neoadjuvant and induction settings. In our previous study, a multivariable analysis indicated that the type of NAC (Gem/Cis vs. Gem/Carbo) had no independent effect on oncological outcomes treated with surgery or CRT [15]. Similarly, Einerhand et al. reported no significant differences in survival outcomes between the two regimens, though pathologic response rates were higher with Gem/Cis [26]. In the present study, the type of NAC (Gem/Cis or Gem/Carbo) likewise had no independent effect on survival endpoints, consistent with these findings.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Our results should be interpreted in light of several limitations. The retrospective and single-arm nature of this study introduces potential selection bias, and treatment heterogeneity may have influenced outcomes. Feasibility outcomes in this study should be interpreted in the context of its retrospective design. The analyzed cohort consisted exclusively of patients who completed NAC and were subsequently considered suitable candidates for CRT. Patients who were unable to complete NAC or who did not proceed to CRT due to early disease progression, treatment-related toxicity, or clinical deterioration were not captured in the analysis. As a result, the true feasibility rates of NAC and subsequent CRT could not be accurately determined, and survivor and selection bias may have led to an overestimation of treatment tolerability and survival outcomes. This limitation is inherent to retrospective studies and should be considered when interpreting the results. In addition, a standardized method of response assessment is needed to ensure consistent and reliable evaluation across studies. Moreover, missing nodal or hydronephrosis data reflect incomplete documentation, particularly in earlier years of the study period, a known limitation of long-term retrospective cohorts. Also, due to incomplete documentation and the absence of standardized fitness metrics, the relative contribution of unfitness versus preference could not be reliably quantified for all patients. Consequently, separation into independent cohorts or inclusion of this variable in multivariable models was not feasible. Despite these limitations, the relatively large cohort size and long follow-up provide meaningful insights into the prognostic factors affecting outcomes in this setting. Our study adds to the cumulative evidence by providing adjusted outcome estimates, highlighting hydronephrosis as a risk marker, and reinforcing the importance of standardized response assessment to guide bladder preservation decisions.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Several areas merit prospective evaluation. First, randomized trials comparing CRT with and without preceding NAC would provide high-quality evidence about the incremental value of NAC in bladder preservation. Also, direct comparison with radical cystectomy in a prospective trial would provide valuable mark in this field. Second, translational studies should evaluate molecular and immunologic biomarkers predictive of cCR and long-term control, including genomic subtypes, DNA damage response signatures, and circulating tumor DNA dynamics; these markers could help tailor systemic therapy and select patients most likely to benefit from organ preservation. Third, given the rapid expansion of immune checkpoint inhibitors for urothelial carcinoma, combination strategies integrating immunotherapy with NAC or with CRT warrant exploration in clinical trials, particularly for cisplatin-ineligible patients. Fourth, harmonization of cCR definitions and standardized surveillance protocols would improve comparability across studies and facilitate meta-analyses [13].

sec.title: Clinical implications
sec.p: For clinicians counseling patients who are medically unfit for cystectomy or who strongly prefer bladder preservation, our data support considering NAC followed by CRT as a feasible option in a multidisciplinary setting, particularly when a robust cCR is achieved. Nevertheless, patients should be informed about the current evidence limitations and the importance of stringent follow-up. Those with adverse features such as hydronephrosis should be counseled about their higher risk profile and the potential need for salvage cystectomy or systemic therapy in the event of recurrence.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study supports the feasibility of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by definitive chemoradiation as a bladder-preserving approach for selected patients with MIBC. cCR is the most important prognostic factor for both OS and EFS and may serve as a surrogate endpoint in future prospective trials. Hydronephrosis remains an adverse prognostic factor and should be incorporated into individualized treatment decisions. Further research, ideally through randomized controlled studies, is needed to clarify the incremental benefit of NAC before CRT and to refine patient selection criteria for bladder preservation strategies.
